title: IUPAC naming
examples: How do I know which part of the molecule is the main chain?
What is the order for naming the functional groups?
If there are two long chains, which one do I choose?

explain.say: Today we learn the IUPAC naming rules for organic compounds. Say the name of the longest continuous carbon chain first. This chain determines the base name of the molecule.
Next, we number the chain to give the lowest possible numbers. These numbers are called locants, and they tell us where things are located.
We must identify the functional group, which is a specific group of atoms. This group takes priority over the main chain name.
The order of priority matters a lot when naming. For example, alcohols take priority over alkanes.
In a real bottle of rubbing alcohol, the functional group is the alcohol part. We name it as an alcohol, not just a simple chain.
A common mistake is forgetting to use the locant number for the functional group. Remember to always state where the special group is attached.

faq.q: If there are multiple functional groups, which one do I name first?
faq.a: You name the group with the highest priority first. This is determined by the IUPAC rules you study. You can also name the lower priority groups.
asks: Which group is the main group name?

faq.q: What if the longest chain has two different functional groups?
faq.a: You still follow the priority rules. The highest priority group dictates the suffix of the name. You use locants for all groups.
asks: Does priority change the chain length?
How do I number if groups are present?

faq.q: Do I always have to find the absolute longest chain?
faq.a: Yes, finding the longest continuous chain is the first step. This gives you the parent name for the molecule.
asks: Is the longest chain always the best choice?
What if two chains are the same length?

faq.q: What does a locant number actually represent?
faq.a: It is simply a number that tells you the exact position of a specific atom or group on the carbon chain. It prevents confusion.
asks: What is the purpose of numbering?
Can I use letters instead of numbers?

faq.q: If I name it wrong, will it still be understood?
faq.a: It might be understood in a lab setting, but for formal chemistry, you must follow IUPAC rules. Correct naming is very important.
asks: Do I need to memorize all rules?

facts: The IUPAC system provides a universal naming convention for organic compounds.
The longest continuous chain forms the parent name of the molecule.
Functional groups, like -OH, have higher naming priority than the parent chain.
Locants are numbers indicating the position of a group on the chain.

quiz.say: What is the primary rule when naming an organic molecule?

options.show: Use the common name if it is shorter.
options.say: Use the common name if it is shorter.

options.show: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain.
options.say: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain.

options.show: Number from the side with the most atoms.
options.say: Number from the side with the most atoms.

quiz.why: This establishes the base name for the entire compound structure.

wrong.0: While common names exist, IUPAC requires standardized systematic naming.
wrong.2: This is tempting because groups are important, but the chain length sets the base name.
wrong.3: This is incorrect; numbering must give the lowest possible locant set.

quiz.say: If a molecule has an alcohol group and a double bond, what is the naming priority?

options.show: The group attached to the first carbon wins.
options.say: The group attached to the first carbon wins.

options.show: The alcohol group takes higher priority.
options.say: The alcohol group takes higher priority.

options.show: The double bond always wins priority.
options.say: The double bond always wins priority.

options.show: The longest chain always wins priority.
options.say: The longest chain always wins priority.

quiz.why: The functional group with the highest priority dictates the main suffix of the name.

wrong.0: The location of the group does not determine its naming priority.
wrong.2: This confuses alkene priority; alcohols often take precedence.
wrong.3: The functional group's inherent priority overrides simple chain length rules.

quiz.say: Given a structure, how do you correctly number the chain?

options.show: Numbering arbitrarily from left to right.
options.say: Numbering arbitrarily from left to right.

options.show: Numbering must give the lowest possible set of locant numbers.
options.say: Numbering must give the lowest possible set of locant numbers.

options.show: Numbering from the end closest to the functional group.
options.say: Numbering from the end closest to the functional group.

options.show: Numbering from the end that has the most carbons.
options.say: Numbering from the end that has the most carbons.

quiz.why: You must check both directions to ensure the smallest numbers appear first.

wrong.0: Arbitrary numbering ignores the rule of achieving the lowest possible locant set.
wrong.2: While this is often true, you must check if the other end gives a lower set overall.
wrong.3: The number of carbons does not determine the correct numbering sequence.
